title: Choose good cases
concept: Testing · typical, edge and unusual cases
description: Pick the test cases a careless average() would trip on: empty lists, decimals, and the last score.

tasks.title: Pick the cases a bug would trip on
tasks.body: One test with an easy value catches few bugs. Good tests mix a typical case, the edges, such as an empty list, a single item or a zero, and unusual values, such as negative numbers.
tasks.detail:
Work out the right answer for each case by hand before running anything. Ask what a careless version might get wrong, such as dividing with //, skipping the last item, or crashing on an empty list, and pick a case that would show it.

For decimals, pick numbers whose answer is exact, such as 7 / 2 = 3.5.

tasks.output: typical, negative and single cases pass
tasks.note: Three kinds of case: a typical list, all negative numbers, and a single item. Each one could catch a different bug.

tasks.question: Which case would show the bug if best started at 0 instead of numbers[0]?
tasks.why: With all negative numbers, none is bigger than 0, so a best that starts at 0 would wrongly return 0.

tasks.prompt: Predict, then run: change best = numbers[0] to best = 0 and see which assert fails. Then add a test for biggest([]) and read the error: what should an empty list give?

The check has a function average(scores) that returns the average of a list of numbers, or 0 for an empty list. Write asserts that test it well.

The check runs them on a correct average(), where they must all pass, and on several broken ones, where at least one must fail for each. Do not write average() yourself.
hints: Start with a typical list whose average you can work out by hand, such as [2, 4], then add the edges.
Which lists would a careless average() get wrong? An empty one, one whose average is not a whole number, and one where the last score makes a difference.
With other names: for total(prices), assert total([]) == 0 tests the empty edge, and assert total([1, 2]) == 3 a typical case.

error_hints.text: A test failed on the correct average(). Work the answer out again by hand, as a decimal: the average of 3 and 4 is 3.5.
average() takes one list: average([2, 4]), with square brackets.
The check provides average(): spell it exactly that way, and do not define it yourself.
Your tests passed on an average() that crashes on an empty list. Test the empty list, [].
Your tests passed on an average() that divides with //. Test a list whose average is not a whole number.
Your tests passed on a broken average(). Check that a change to the last score changes your answer.
Your tests passed on a broken average(). Test lists with more than one score.

similar_example.code:
def total(prices):
    result = 0
    for p in prices:
        result = result + p
    return result

assert total([]) == 0
assert total([1, 2]) == 3
assert total([5]) == 5
print("total() passed")
similar_example.note: The empty, typical and single cases for a total. Your tests are for average(), which can go wrong in more ways.

other_ways.code:
import math
assert average([]) == 0
assert average([2, 4]) == 3
assert average([3, 4]) == 3.5
assert math.isclose(average([1, 2, 2]), 5 / 3)
assert average([10, 0, 5]) == 5
other_ways.note: math.isclose() compares decimals that cannot be written exactly, such as five thirds.
